newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: President says U.S. treats Colombians as criminals.
newsitem.headline: President says U.S. treats Colombians as criminals.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper condemned outspoken U.S. ambassador Myles Frechette for treating all Colombians as "latent criminals" who needed to be taught a lesson between right and wrong, in an interview with Colombia's leading daily Sunday.

"It makes me very angry that he (Frechette) presents all Colombians as latent criminals who need to be pressured into understanding what is good and bad or honourable and dishonourable," Samper told El Tiempo newspaper.

Frechette is not known for mincing his words and has made direct calls to the government, Congress and private business sectors to crack down harder on the country's drug kingpins -- prompting Colombian politicians to complain of foreign meddling in internal affairs.
The battle between the U.S. envoy and Samper, under fire at home and abroad for allegedly funding his 1994 election campaign with drug money, became increasingly personal in 1996.

The United States decertified Colombia as an ally in the drug war in March. It followed up by stripping Samper of his U.S. entry visa in the summer, citing his known ties with drug lords even though an inquiry in Colombia's Congress cleared him of any wrongdoing.
Frechette has rarely missed an opportunity to bully Samper into pushing tougher anti-drug laws through Congress under the threat of U.S. economic sanctions.
In late October, he publicly criticised as insufficient bills then being debated by Congress to lift Colombia's 5-year-old ban on extradition and to strip drug lords of their illicit fortunes.
"If there was one difficult moment in the passage of those bills through Congress it was when, with all respect to the ambassador, he tried to poke his nose in," Samper said.

The U.S. envoy grudgingly congratulated Congress for finally approving a law 10 days ago that will empower the government to seize drug-related assets accumulated over the last 20 years. But he did not rule out sanctions nor even less hint that the move would help Colombia regain certification in March 1997.

The new law and last week's appointment of Defence Minister Juan Carlos Esguerra to the vacant post of ambassador to Washington are, however, widely expected to improve Samper's strained relations with the Clinton administration.
But Samper warned: "Relations cannot be reduced to some kind of operational agenda for the war on drugs. Relations must have a political context."
